title: Our position on open-weights models
gist: Dario Amodei publicly disowns any Anthropic support for banning Chinese open-weights models, calling such bans protectionism that misses the real risks, and instead names three policy asks: hard chip export controls plus anti-smuggling enforcement, targeted crackdowns on industrial-scale distillation, and mandatory pre-release safety testing for all sufficiently capable models regardless of origin or openness. He breaks with the industry open letter on the claim that open access inherently favors defenders, arguing biology likely has a structural attacker advantage.

insights.claim: Anthropic states it has never advocated a ban on open-weights models, responding directly to accusations that it wants such a ban to protect its own commercial position after reports that US officials are weighing barring US companies from using Chinese open-weights models.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The largest safety-positioned lab is publicly off the ban trade; policy risk to firms building on Chinese open-weights inference is lower than the headline debate implies.
insights.quote: Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models.
insights.locator: Over the last few days there has been

insights.claim: Open-weights models without dangerous capabilities are framed as a public good whose only cost is the compute needed to run them, delivering value to businesses, developers and researchers.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Reinforces that the marginal cost of frontier-adjacent intelligence collapses toward compute — value accrues to inference/compute providers, not to model licensing, for the commoditized tier.
insights.quote: Open-weights models that don’t have dangerous capabilities are a public good: they don’t cost anything besides the compute needed to run them, and they provide value to businesses, developers, and researchers.
insights.locator: Open-weights models that don’t have dangerous capabilities

insights.claim: A ban on US business use of foreign open-weights models would fail on its own terms because bad actors are unlikely to be legitimate US businesses, so the only real effect would be shielding US AI companies from competition.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Explicitly separates safety policy from protectionism — watch for US labs whose policy asks fail this test as a tell for regulatory-moat strategies.
insights.quote: It would protect US AI companies from competition, but that has never been my goal.
insights.locator: But banning the use of these models by US businesses

themes.theme: Two nightmare scenarios as the real threat model

insights.claim: The primary stated national-security concern is authoritarian governments — with the CCP the most capable threat but not the only one — building AI more powerful than US models and using it for permanent military superiority or deep domestic repression.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Frames AI policy as a state-capability race, not a product-safety debate — supports persistent bipartisan support for export controls and defense-adjacent AI spend.
insights.locator: My primary concern is the risk that authoritarian governments

insights.claim: Whether a dangerous model is open or closed is argued to be irrelevant to the state-competition threat, and the single most dangerous model may be one trained in secret and given only to the People's Liberation Army for drones and to the Ministry of State Security for surveillance.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Implies the policy fight moves upstream to training inputs (chips, data, distillation) rather than to model distribution rules — position for controls on compute, not on downloads.
insights.quote: the most dangerous model may be one that is trained in secret and handed only to the People’s Liberation Army for use in drones and the Ministry of State Security for surveillance and repression
insights.locator: In fact, the most dangerous model may be one

insights.claim: The essay cites Vice President Vance's Paris warning that authoritarian regimes have stolen and used AI to strengthen military, intelligence and surveillance capabilities, and the Intelligence Community's 2026 Annual Threat Assessment finding that other global powers' AI progress is challenging US economic competitiveness, as evidence the concern is already US government consensus.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Official US threat language is already aligned with restriction — durable policy tailwind for domestic compute buildout and export enforcement across administrations.
insights.quote: other global powers’ robust progress in AI is challenging US economic competitiveness and national security advantages
insights.locator: This concern is widely shared within the US government

insights.claim: The secondary concern is misuse of powerful models for cyber or biological attacks plus serious alignment problems, where open weights do plausibly carry higher risk because guardrails are hard to apply, usage is hard to monitor, and released weights cannot be withdrawn.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The irreversibility argument is the durable case for pre-release gating — any future incident traced to open weights would hit the whole open-model ecosystem at once.
insights.quote: once weights are released they cannot be withdrawn
insights.locator: My secondary concern is the risk that powerful AI models

insights.claim: A UK AI Security Institute report is cited for the claim that open-weight release of models with dangerous capabilities creates a persistent and irreversible misuse risk because safeguards can be removed and copies redistributed beyond monitoring.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Third-party state safety institutes are supplying the evidentiary base for future rules — their publications are a leading indicator of regulatory direction.
insights.quote: For models with dangerous capabilities – including highly cyber-capable models – open weight release therefore creates a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse.
insights.locator: Footnotes: See this report from the UK AI Security Institute

themes.theme: Chips as the binding constraint via scaling laws

insights.claim: The central policy ask is to withhold powerful chips and chipmaking equipment from China and to crack down on rampant smuggling and workarounds, because China's limited domestic production capacity means scaling laws prevent it from building more powerful models than the US without US chips.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Continued or tightened export controls plus enforcement actions are the base case; smuggling crackdowns are a tail risk for grey-market channel revenue and a tailwind for compliant domestic capacity.
insights.quote: China has limited domestic production capacity, and therefore, due to the scaling laws, cannot build more powerful models than the US without US chips.
insights.locator: We should not sell powerful chips or chipmaking equipment to China

insights.claim: Chip denial is presented as the most efficient and direct block on the authoritarian-frontier threat and as an indirect mitigant of the misuse threat, because it hampers the training of models that sit outside the reach of US law.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Compute chokepoints, not model distribution rules, are where policy leverage concentrates — the export-control regime is the highest-beta variable for the AI supply chain.
insights.locator: This is the most efficient and direct way to block threat #1

insights.claim: Industrial-scale distillation is identified as the main way China partially evades chip bans, because distillation is far more compute-efficient than training from scratch and lets Chinese labs build much better models than their chip count would ordinarily allow.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Frontier labs' pricing power depends on plugging this leak; API access controls and anti-distillation policy are the next regulatory frontier after chips.
insights.locator: We should crack down on industrial-scale distillation operations

insights.claim: Distillation is judged insufficient to give the CCP equivalent or superior capability to the US, but sufficient to bring the Chinese frontier to within a few months of the US frontier.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A quantified capability gap of only a few months caps how long any US model advantage can be monetized at premium prices — margin compression risk for closed frontier APIs.
insights.quote: Distillation does not allow the CCP to obtain equivalent or superior AI capabilities to the US, but it can bring the Chinese frontier to within a few months of the US frontier.
insights.locator: Distillation does not allow the CCP to obtain

insights.claim: The relevant objection to distillation operations is said to be state backing by an authoritarian government seeking to overtake the US frontier, not the fact that many of those operators release open weights — so a blanket open-weights ban is the wrong remedy.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Expect targeted legal and commercial frameworks aimed at specific actors rather than category-wide bans — narrower blast radius for open-model infrastructure businesses.
insights.locator: It is true that many of the companies carrying out these operations

insights.claim: Anthropic admits its own anti-distillation enforcement is structurally limited: offending accounts can often only be identified after substantial distillation has already occurred, and distillers spin up large numbers of fake accounts that form a moving target, which is why company practice alone cannot solve the problem.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A candid admission that model-weight value leaks faster than detection — supports the view that frontier capability leads are short-lived and that regulation, not vendor controls, is the only durable fix.
insights.quote: the relevant accounts can often only be identified after substantial distillation has occurred, and distillation often involves creating large numbers of fake accounts that form a moving target
insights.locator: Footnotes: At Anthropic we’re committed to cracking down

themes.theme: Mandatory pre-release safety testing as the emerging consensus

insights.claim: The proposed remedy for misuse risk is mandatory safety testing for cyber, biological and alignment risks on all sufficiently capable models before release, open or closed, with less capable models from startups and academia exempted entirely.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A capability-threshold regime concentrates compliance cost on the largest labs while sparing the long tail — regulatory burden scales with model size, a mild moat for incumbents at the frontier.
insights.locator: All sufficiently capable models, open and closed

insights.claim: Mandatory capability-threshold testing is described as close to consensus, with the Trump administration having moved in this direction in recent months and recent industry proposals applying testing regardless of country of origin or open/closed status.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Pre-release testing mandates are the most likely piece of US AI regulation to actually land — build compliance and evals capacity ahead of it.
insights.locator: I think this idea is actually close to a consensus

insights.claim: Whether open models pose increased risk and whether that risk is mitigable should be settled empirically by testing rather than decided in advance, with Anthropic's recent research on modular training strategies cited as a promising route to safer open-weights models.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Leaves the door open for a technically sanctioned safe-open-weights path — a research direction to watch as it would defuse the whole policy fight.
insights.quote: Whether open models do or don’t pose an increased risk, and whether that risk can be mitigated, is something that should emerge from testing, rather than be decided in advance
insights.locator: Whether open models do or don’t pose an increased risk

insights.claim: Effective safety testing is said to require global scope including CCP buy-in, which is judged possibly achievable because limited cooperation on preventing AI biological weapons is in China's own interest.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A narrow US-China AI arms-control channel on bioweapons is a live, underpriced diplomatic scenario despite the otherwise adversarial framing.
insights.quote: Note that to be effective, testing would need to be global, which means even the CCP would need to be on board.
insights.locator: Note that to be effective, testing would need to be global

themes.theme: Breaking with the open letter on offense-defense balance

insights.claim: The essay agrees with much of the industry open letter — open weights expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition for some use cases and give customers greater control — but rejects its assertions that open weights necessarily ease safeguard development or that broad capability access necessarily helps defenders more than attackers.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Marks the fault line inside the AI industry coalition: access-and-competition arguments are conceded, offense-defense arguments are not — expect the policy fight to concentrate there.
insights.quote: But I don’t agree with the letter’s assertions that open-weights models necessarily make it easier to develop safeguards or that broad access to capabilities necessarily helps defenders more than attackers.
insights.locator: This brings me to the open letter

insights.claim: Biology is argued to have a strong attacker-defender asymmetry: sufficiently capable models may quickly weaponize pandemic-level viruses using widely available materials, whereas defense is a multi-year operational task even in the best case, as Operation Warp Speed showed.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Bio is the domain where a capability threshold triggers the harshest regulation — biosecurity, DNA synthesis screening and rapid-response countermeasures are the structurally favored policy spend.
insights.locator: For example, I worry that biology will have a strong attacker-defender asymmetry

insights.claim: The underlying mental model is that biological safety today rests on a negative correlation between intellectual capability and desire to commit catastrophic harm — a correlation internet search and DNA synthesis were never powerful enough to break, but which AI is expected to break very soon at its current rate of progress.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable trigger condition for step-change AI regulation: the first demonstration that models decouple capability from intent would reprice the entire policy environment.
insights.quote: what I believe currently keeps us safe in biology is not “defenders”, or even the availability of materials, but a negative correlation between intellectual capability and desire to commit catastrophic harm
insights.locator: Footnotes: See Section 2 of The Adolescence of Technology
